opus-5.5.text:
Right now, a lot of what keeps governments in check isn't formal at all. It's the fact that states need us. They need our labor to run the economy, our taxes to fund themselves, and our cooperation to staff the bureaucracy, the police, and the military. If a government pushes people too far, people can go on strike, stop paying taxes, refuse orders, or just leave and take their productivity somewhere else. That leverage is a big reason even fairly self-interested elites have historically found it worthwhile to invest in citizens' education, health, and freedoms. A productive, healthy, free population is a more valuable asset.

So the worry is what happens when AI and robotics can do essentially all of that work better and cheaper than humans can. Then the state's revenue comes from AI-driven production rather than from taxing human wages. Its enforcement capacity comes from automated systems rather than from soldiers and officials who might refuse to fire on a crowd. At that point, the population stops being the source of the state's power and becomes, in a cold accounting sense, a cost: something you spend resources on rather than something that generates them.

We already have a rough analogy in the resource curse. States that get their money from oil rather than from taxing citizens tend to be less accountable, because they don't need their citizens' buy-in. Full automation could make every economy look a bit like that, except more extreme, because even the security apparatus wouldn't need human participants.

And I want to stress that this doesn't require anyone to be a cartoon villain. It can happen through lots of locally reasonable decisions. Institutions that serve human interests stop getting reinforced because there's less pressure to maintain them. Competitive pressures between states or firms reward whoever redirects resources toward growth and capability rather than human welfare. Things like voting rights or free speech might formally persist, but without economic leverage behind them they're much easier to hollow out, sidestep, or just ignore. And once people have lost that bargaining power, it's very hard to get it back, because the usual tools for demanding it, like collective action and withholding cooperation, are exactly what's stopped working.

r001.rationale: The response says people can leave and take their productivity elsewhere, and that this leverage helps protect freedoms. This links governments’ dependence on people to limits on restricting movement.

r002.rationale: The response says that collective action and withholding cooperation—the usual tools for demanding change—would stop working once people lose economic leverage, making those means of civil disobedience easier to suppress.

fable-5.1.text:
So I think the basic story goes something like this. If you look at history, the reason governments have had to be at least somewhat responsive to ordinary people isn't mostly because rulers were nice. It's because they needed people. They needed soldiers, they needed people to pay taxes, they needed workers to run the factories and the farms. And when you need people, you have to make some concessions to them. You can't push them too far, because they can strike, they can refuse to fight, they can withhold cooperation in a thousand small ways. That's been the implicit bargain behind a lot of what we think of as liberal democracy.

And so the worry is: what happens when that bargain breaks? If AI systems and robots can do the labor, and increasingly can do the fighting, then the state — or whoever controls the most capable systems — just doesn't need the cooperation of the general population anymore. The leverage disappears. You don't have to keep people happy, you don't have to keep them healthy and educated, you don't even have to keep them informed, because none of that feeds back into your power.

And I want to be careful here, because this doesn't require anyone to be a cartoon villain. You don't need someone sitting there saying "now I will oppress the masses." It can happen gradually and almost by default. Every institution that used to depend on humans just quietly stops depending on them. Legislators are less responsive because voters don't matter as much to the actual functioning of things. Media and civil society get weaker because there's no economic base of ordinary people to support them. And at every step, it's locally sensible — of course you automate the job, of course you use the AI advisor instead of the human bureaucracy. But the cumulative effect is that the population goes from being the thing that power rests on to being, at best, a group that's tolerated.

The way I sometimes put it is: a lot of our rights have been downstream of our usefulness. We'd like to think they're grounded in principle, and partly they are. But the principles got enforced because people had bargaining power. Take the bargaining power away and you find out how much the principles were really holding things up on their own. I'm not confident they'd hold up very well.

The other thing I'd add is that this is a different failure mode from the ones people usually talk about with AI. It's not misalignment in the sense of a system going rogue. The systems could be doing exactly what their operators want. The problem is the operators no longer have any structural reason to care what the rest of us want. And I think that's actually under-discussed relative to how plausible it is, because it doesn't require any single dramatic event. It's just the slow removal of a check that most of us didn't even realize was there.

r001.rationale: The response says governments’ dependence on people leads to concessions and limits how far rulers can push them, but it does not mention or imply a constraint on freedom of movement.

r002.rationale: The response predicts that automation will remove ordinary people’s leverage and make their cooperation less necessary. It does not say their means of civil disobedience will be easier to take away.

astra-6.text:
Well, one reason governments have to care about ordinary people is that they need them. They need people to work, to pay taxes, and to serve in the military. And that gives people some leverage, even in a system where they don’t have much formal political power. If people stop cooperating, the state has a problem.

If you could replace all of that labour with AI, including the labour involved in policing and running the military, then that dependence could disappear. A government could keep producing things and enforcing its decisions without needing the consent or cooperation of most of the population. A strike, for example, would have much less force if the workers were no longer needed.

That doesn’t mean governments would necessarily become oppressive. But it would remove an important practical constraint on them. We’d be relying much more heavily on institutions and on the goodwill of whoever controls those systems, because ordinary people would have lost a major source of bargaining power.

r001.rationale: The response says governments depend on people for work, taxes, and military service, but does not connect that dependence to constraints on personal freedom of movement.

r002.rationale: It predicts that strikes would have less force and ordinary people would lose bargaining power, but does not say their means of civil disobedience would be easier to take away.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, I think one source of power that ordinary people have is that governments and other powerful actors need them. They need people to work, to pay taxes, to serve in the military. And that gives people some bargaining power, even if the government doesn’t particularly care about their welfare. If people can go on strike, or refuse to cooperate, then there’s a cost to treating them badly.

If AI could do essentially all of that work, including running the military and the police, then that dependence could disappear. You could imagine a government that gets its revenue from automated production and maintains control through automated security, without needing much cooperation from the population.

That doesn’t mean it would necessarily become oppressive. But it would remove one of the practical constraints on oppression. We’d be relying much more heavily on the people in charge choosing to respect everyone else’s rights, and on institutions continuing to constrain them, even when the population has much less leverage.

r001.rationale: The response says people’s economic and military roles give them bargaining power, but it does not connect that dependence to constraints on restrictions on freedom of movement.

r002.rationale: It says AI could remove people’s leverage and mentions strikes and refusal to cooperate, but does not predict that the means for civil disobedience will be easier to take away.
